title: Introduction
intro: A program is a set of instructions a computer follows. Python lets you express those instructions using readable words and symbols. In this lab, you will write code, run it, and use the output to check your thinking.
steps: Write an instruction with print().
Put the message inside matching quotation marks.
Run the program. Python displays the message without the quotation marks.
pitfall: Python is case-sensitive: Print and print are different names.

title: Get Started
intro: The Python interpreter executes your code. A saved Python program usually has a .py extension. This portal includes an interpreter, so you can practice without installing anything.
steps: Write one statement on each line.
The interpreter runs the first line before the second.
Read the output from top to bottom.
pitfall: Click Run code to execute your work; simply typing does not run it.

title: Syntax
intro: Syntax is the set of rules for writing valid code. Python uses indentation to group instructions. After a line that ends in a colon, indent its block consistently, usually with four spaces.
steps: Write the condition and end it with a colon.
Indent the statement belonging to the condition.
Return to the left edge when the block ends.
pitfall: Mixing indentation levels can produce an IndentationError.

title: Output
intro: print() displays text, numbers, or the result of a calculation. Text needs quotation marks. Numbers and arithmetic expressions do not. Multiple values are separated by a space unless you set sep.
steps: Pass text in quotes to print().
Pass a calculation without quotes to evaluate it.
Use separate print() calls for separate lines.
pitfall: print("12 + 8") prints the expression as text instead of calculating it.

title: Comments
intro: A comment explains code for people reading it. Python ignores text following # outside a string. Useful comments explain the purpose of a step rather than repeating the statement.
steps: Start a comment with #.
Keep the instruction on its own line or before the comment.
Run the program: only the instruction affects output.
pitfall: A # inside a quoted string is ordinary text, not a comment.

title: Variables
intro: A variable is a name that refers to a value. Use = to assign a value and use the name to retrieve it. Choose meaningful names such as course_name. Names cannot start with a number or contain spaces.
steps: Assign a value to a descriptive name.
Use that name later without quotation marks.
Assign a new value when the information changes.
pitfall: The = sign assigns a value; == compares two values.

title: Data Types
intro: Every value has a type. Common types include int for whole numbers, float for decimals, str for text, and bool for True or False. The type determines which operations make sense.
steps: Create a value.
Call type(value) to inspect its type.
Use type(value).__name__ for just the type’s name.
pitfall: "True" is a string; True without quotes is a Boolean.

title: Numbers
intro: Python has integers, floating-point numbers, and complex numbers. Arithmetic works on numeric values. Division with / produces a float, while // performs floor division.
steps: Choose int for counts and float for measurements.
Combine numbers using arithmetic operators.
Print the result and check whether it matches your estimate.
pitfall: Floating-point calculations can have tiny rounding differences.

title: Casting
intro: Casting converts a value to another type. int() converts suitable values to integers, float() creates floating-point numbers, and str() creates text. Conversion succeeds only when the value has a suitable form.
steps: Begin with a value in one type.
Call the conversion function.
Use the converted value in the operation you need.
pitfall: int("18.5") fails; float("18.5") works.

title: Strings
intro: A string is a sequence of characters. Indexes start at zero. A slice [start:stop] includes start and excludes stop. Methods such as .upper(), .lower(), and .strip() return new strings.
steps: Create text with matching quotes.
Select characters with indexing or slicing.
Use a method to transform the text.
pitfall: Strings are immutable: a method returns a new string rather than changing the original.

title: Booleans
intro: A Boolean is True or False. Comparisons produce Boolean values, which help programs make decisions. The first letters of True and False must be capitalized.
steps: Create or compare values.
Read the comparison as a question.
Store or print the True/False answer.

title: Operators
intro: Operators perform calculations and comparisons. % gives a remainder, ** raises a power, and and/or/not combine Boolean expressions. Parentheses make the intended order easier to read.
steps: Identify the calculation or comparison you need.
Choose the appropriate operator.
Use parentheses when combining operations.
pitfall: Use == for comparison and = for assignment.

title: Lists
intro: A list stores an ordered, changeable collection. Use square brackets to create one. Access items by index and use append() to add an item. Slices, loops, and comprehensions help process several items.
steps: Create a list using square brackets.
Access or update an item by its zero-based index.
Add an item with append() and inspect the result.
pitfall: The last valid index is len(list) - 1.

title: Tuples
intro: A tuple is an ordered collection whose item references cannot be changed after creation. Tuples are useful for fixed groups such as coordinates. Unpacking assigns their items to separate names.
steps: Create a tuple with comma-separated items.
Unpack it into the same number of variables.
Use those variables as ordinary values.
example:
point = (4, 7)
x, y = point
print(x + y)
pitfall: A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: (5,).

title: Sets
intro: A set stores unique items without a reliable display order. It is useful for removing duplicates and comparing membership. Union combines items; intersection finds items shared by both sets.
steps: Create a set from a list or with braces.
Use a set operation such as & for intersection.
Use sorted() when you need predictable printed order.
pitfall: {} creates an empty dictionary. Use set() for an empty set.

title: Dictionaries
intro: A dictionary maps keys to values. Use a meaningful key to look up a value, rather than a numerical position. Keys are unique. Values can be changed and new key/value pairs can be added.
steps: Create key: value pairs inside braces.
Read a value with dictionary[key].
Assign to a key to update or add information.
pitfall: A missing key raises KeyError; .get() lets you supply a default.

title: If…Else
intro: Conditional statements choose which block to run. if checks the first condition, elif checks another when needed, and else handles the remaining case. Only the first matching branch runs.
steps: Write if followed by a condition and colon.
Indent the instructions for that case.
Add elif or else when there are other outcomes.
pitfall: An else branch has no condition after it.

title: Match
intro: match compares a value against several patterns. Each case describes a possible match. The wildcard _ handles any value not matched earlier. match requires Python 3.10 or later.
steps: Place the value after match.
Write a case for each recognized value.
Finish with case _ for a fallback.
example:
day = 2
match day:
    case 1:
        print("Monday")
    case 2:
        print("Tuesday")
    case _:
        print("Another day")
pitfall: A bare variable name in a case can capture a value instead of comparing with an existing variable.

exercises.title: Guided practice

    case "stop":
        print("Finished")
    case _:

exercises.hint: String patterns need quotation marks.

title: While Loops
intro: A while loop repeats a block while its condition is true. Update the value controlling the condition so the loop eventually stops. break exits a loop early; continue moves to the next iteration.
steps: Initialize a counter before the loop.
Test its value in the while condition.
Update the counter inside the loop.
pitfall: A condition that never becomes false causes an infinite loop. Use Stop if needed.

title: For Loops

steps: Choose the collection to process.
Use for item in collection followed by a colon.
Indent the action to repeat for each item.
pitfall: Changing a collection while iterating over it can lead to unexpected behavior.

steps: Define the function and its parameters.
Compute a result inside the indented body.
Call the function and use its returned value.

steps: Give each required input a parameter.
Provide a default for an optional input.
Call with positional or keyword arguments.

title: *args and **kwargs
intro: *args collects extra positional arguments in a tuple. **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments in a dictionary. These let a function accept a flexible number of values.
steps: Put *args or **kwargs in the parameter list.
Treat args as a tuple and kwargs as a dictionary.
Loop over the values or access a named keyword.

title: Scope
intro: Scope determines where a name can be used. A name assigned inside a function is usually local to that function. A name assigned at the top level is global to the module. Prefer passing values and returning results to changing globals.
steps: Identify the enclosing function or module.
Use a local name for temporary calculations.
Return the local result when the caller needs it.
example:
label = "outside"
def show():
    label = "inside"
    print(label)
show()
print(label)
pitfall: Assigning a local value does not automatically modify a global value with the same name.

title: Decorators
intro: A decorator receives a function and returns a replacement function. It can add behavior before or after a call. The @ syntax applies the decorator when the function is defined.
steps: Write a function that accepts another function.
Return a wrapper that calls the original function.
Place @decorator above the function to decorate.
pitfall: Returning wrapper() executes immediately; returning wrapper returns the callable.

steps: Write lambda and its parameters.

Call the function or pass it to another function.

title: Recursion
intro: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem. It must have a base case that returns without another recursive call. Each recursive step should move closer to the base case.
steps: Define the simplest case first.
Return immediately for that base case.
Reduce the problem in the recursive call.
pitfall: A missing base case eventually causes RecursionError.

title: Generators
intro: A generator yields values one at a time. Calling a function containing yield creates a generator object. Iteration resumes the function where it last paused, which can avoid building a large list.
steps: Define a function containing yield.
Yield one result at each step.
Use a loop or list() to consume the generator.
example:
def first_three():
    yield 1
    yield 2
    yield 3

print(list(first_three()))
pitfall: A generator is consumed as you iterate; call the function again for a fresh one.

Choose the step, if it is not one.

Access the resulting dictionary or list.

title: RegEx

Use findall() to collect all matches.
pitfall: A pattern is not ordinary substring text; symbols such as . and * have special meanings.

title: Try…Except
intro: Exceptions report problems that occur while code runs. try contains the risky operation. except handles a specific error so the program can respond. finally runs cleanup whether an exception occurs or not.
steps: Put the operation inside try.
Catch the specific expected exception.
Give a useful fallback message or value.
pitfall: Catching every exception can hide unrelated programming mistakes.

Add a format specification when needed.

title: None
intro: None represents the absence of a value. It is different from zero, an empty string, and False. A function with no explicit return value returns None. Compare with None using is or is not.
steps: Use None when a value is not yet available.

Handle the missing-value case before using the value.

title: Virtual Environments
intro: A virtual environment keeps a project’s Python packages separate from those of other projects. Create one in a local terminal with python -m venv .venv, then activate it before installing packages. This browser lab already has an isolated runtime.

Activate it: Windows uses .venv\Scripts\activate; macOS/Linux uses source .venv/bin/activate.
Install project packages while the environment is active.
pitfall: Virtual environments are local folders; do not commit the folder to Git.

title: Object-Oriented Programming
intro: Object-oriented programming groups data and behavior. A class defines a kind of object. An instance is one particular object created from that class. This can help model students, courses, or bank accounts.
steps: Identify the kind of thing to model.
Define a class for its shared structure.
Create an instance and access its information.
example:
class Course:
    subject = "Python"

course = Course()
print(course.subject)
pitfall: A class is the definition; an instance is an object made from it.

title: Classes and Objects
intro: Classes define attributes and methods that their instances can use. Calling the class creates an object. Dot notation accesses an attribute on a class or an instance.
steps: Define the class with class Name:.
Create an instance by calling Name().
Access an attribute through object.attribute.
example:
class Lab:
    room = 405

lab = Lab()
print(lab.room)
pitfall: Assigning badge = Badge references the class; Badge() creates an instance.

steps: Define __init__(self, ...).

Pass the required values when creating the object.

title: self Parameter

steps: Make self the method’s first parameter.
Read an attribute through self.attribute.
Call the method on the object without passing self yourself.
pitfall: Forgetting self in an instance method usually causes an argument-count error.

title: Class Properties
intro: Attributes store object data. A class attribute belongs to the class and can be shared; an instance attribute belongs to a particular object. Assigning self.name in __init__ gives each instance its own name.
steps: Use a class attribute for a shared fact.
Use instance attributes for per-object data.
Read both through an instance when appropriate.
pitfall: A mutable class attribute, such as a list, can be shared unexpectedly between instances.

title: Polymorphism
intro: Polymorphism lets different objects respond to the same operation in their own way. Code can call a shared method name without checking each object’s exact class, as long as the objects support that method.
steps: Give different classes the same method name.
Create instances of those classes.
Call that method in a shared loop.

title: Encapsulation
intro: Encapsulation keeps data and the methods that manage it together. A leading underscore signals an internal attribute by convention. Properties can control access. These conventions organize code; they are not a security boundary.
steps: Store internal data in an attribute.

Keep validation close to the data it protects.
pitfall: An underscore signals intent; it does not make data secret.

title: File Handling
intro: open() creates a file object. The mode selects reading, writing, or appending. A with block closes the file automatically. Files in this browser lab live in a temporary virtual filesystem, separate from your computer.
steps: Open the file with an explicit mode.
Read or write within a with block.
Use the file’s contents before the block ends.
example:
with open("note.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Practice daily")
with open("note.txt") as file:
    print(file.read())
pitfall: Opening with "w" replaces existing file contents.

title: Read Files
intro: read() gets the remaining file contents as one string. readline() reads a line; iterating over a file processes its lines. strip() can remove newline characters from each line when appropriate.
steps: Open an existing file in read mode.
Read the whole file or iterate line by line.
Process the returned strings.
example:
with open("tasks.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Read\nCode")
with open("tasks.txt") as file:
    for line in file:
        print(line.strip())
pitfall: File contents arrive as strings even when they contain digits.

title: Write and Create Files
intro: Mode "w" creates or replaces a file; "a" appends to it; "x" creates it only if it does not already exist. write() does not automatically add a newline, so include one when needed.

Read it back to verify the result.

with open("log.txt", "a") as file:
    file.write(" entry")
with open("log.txt") as file:
    print(file.read())
pitfall: Using "w" for the second operation would erase Hello.

title: Delete Files
intro: The os module can remove a file with os.remove(). Check os.path.exists() if absence is expected. Deleting a file removes its contents, so only delete the specific file you intend. This exercise uses temporary browser files.
steps: Import os.
Check whether the named file exists.
Remove it and verify that it is gone.
example:
import os
with open("temporary.txt", "w") as file:
    file.write("Temporary")
os.remove("temporary.txt")
print(os.path.exists("temporary.txt"))
pitfall: Removing a nonexistent file raises FileNotFoundError.
